title: Traffic Light Game
strapline: Red stop, green go, amber get ready — a running game that teaches a rule worth knowing.
intent: Children develop listening skills and the self-control to stop a moving body on a signal.
Children learn what traffic lights mean, which is genuine road-safety knowledge.
Stopping and starting on cue is real self-regulation practice, disguised as a game.
Moving as different vehicles builds imagination alongside gross motor control.
Turn-taking as the person who holds the lights builds confidence and fairness.
implementation: Play a stop-and-go game: red means stop, green means go, amber means get ready.
Use real coloured cards or discs so the signal is visual as well as spoken.
Let children move around the space as different vehicles — cars, buses, bikes, trains.
Model the actions clearly and reinforce the safety language: stop, wait, go, look.
Vary the pace and hold red for longer sometimes — waiting is the hard part.
Hand the lights to a child once the game is established so they lead it.
Connect the game explicitly to real crossings the children use on the way in.
key_questions: What does red mean? What should your body do?
Why do you think we have traffic lights on real roads?
Can you be a bus this time instead of a car?
What is the hardest part — going or stopping?
Where have you seen traffic lights near your home?

impact.text: Children run, stop and negotiate space with control and confidence.
Children listen and respond in a group and shift attention on a signal.
Children regulate themselves and keep to an agreed rule.
Children take turns, including waiting for the turn to lead.
Children know their local patch and the rules that keep them safe in it.
Children take up and use the safety vocabulary in their own play.

enhancements: A painted road on the playground with a real zebra crossing to practise on.
A child-made set of traffic lights from boxes and coloured cellophane.
A road-safety walk to a real crossing near the setting.
A ride-on version using the bikes and trikes rather than running.
A "sleeping traffic" variation where amber means creep very slowly.
A high-visibility jacket and lollipop role-play extension.

playing_exploring: Children choose their vehicle and how it moves.
The game is physical, immediate and open to everyone.
active_learning: Children concentrate hard on the signal across a whole game.
Stopping a running body takes real effort and they build it.
creating_thinking: Children connect the game to real roads and real rules.
They anticipate the change of light and prepare for it.
